<!-- Generated by cmd/nomi-docgen from tests/exercism/robot-name. Edit the exercise, not this page. -->

Give each robot off the factory floor a random name of two uppercase letters and three digits, give it a new one when it is reset, and never give two robots the same name.

Adapted from Exercism's [problem specification](https://github.com/exercism/problem-specifications/tree/main/exercises/robot-name) (MIT). Listed under [Games & Simulation](/examples/?subject=games-and-simulation).

```nomi-run
// FILE: robot_name.nomi
import std/random.{Generator, Seed}

once letters = Iter.to_vector('A'..='Z')

/// How many names there are: two letters, then three digits.
once name_count = 26 * 26 * 1000

/// A robot and the name it answers to.
pub opaque struct Robot {
    name: String
}

impl Robot {
    /// The robot's name: two uppercase letters and three digits, as `RX837`.
    pub fn name(robot: Robot) -> String {
        robot.name
    }
}

/// Why the factory cannot name another robot.
pub enum Error {
    NamesExhausted
}

/// A factory that names robots at random and never gives two the same
/// name. It is a value: each robot it builds or resets answers the factory
/// after it, holding every name given so far and the seed to draw from next.
pub opaque struct Factory {
    seed: Seed
    given: Set<String>
}

impl Factory {
    /// A factory that draws names from `seed`.
    pub fn new(seed: Seed) -> Factory {
        #Factory{seed, given: %[]}
    }

    /// A new robot with a name no robot of this factory has had, or
    /// `NamesExhausted` when every name has been given.
    pub fn build(factory: Factory) -> Result<#(Robot, Factory), Error> {
        if Set.size(factory.given) == name_count {
            return Err(.NamesExhausted)
        }

        #(name, seed) = Generator.step(names(), factory.seed)

        if Set.contains?(factory.given, name) {
            Factory.build(#{..factory, seed})
        } else {
            Ok(#(#Robot{name}, #Factory{seed, given: Set.insert(factory.given, name)}))
        }
    }

    /// `robot` reset to its factory settings: wiped, and named again with a
    /// name no robot of this factory has had. The old name is not given
    /// again.
    pub fn reset(factory: Factory, _robot: Robot) -> Result<#(Robot, Factory), Error> {
        Factory.build(factory)
    }
}

/// Every name, each equally likely: a number below `name_count` read as two
/// letters and three digits.
fn names() -> Generator<String> {
    Generator.int(0, name_count - 1)
    |> Generator.map(fn n -> {
        first = Vector.at(letters, n / 26_000)
        second = Vector.at(letters, n / 1000 % 26)
        digits = Int.to_string(n % 1000) |> String.pad_start(3, "0")
        String.from_codepoints([first, second]) + digits
    })
}

// FILE: robot_name_test.nomi
import {
    std/random.Seed
    robot_name.{Factory, Robot}
}

/// Whether `name` is two uppercase letters and three digits.
fn well_formed?(name: String) -> Bool {
    case String.to_codepoints(name) {
        [a, b, c, d, e] -> {
            letter? = &Range.contains?('A'..='Z', &1)
            Iter.all?([a, b], letter?) and Iter.all?([c, d, e], Codepoint.digit?)
        }

        _ ->
            False
    }
}

/// The names of `count` robots from `factory`, in the order it built them.
fn names(factory: Factory, count: Int) -> List<String> {
    #(names, _factory) =
        1..=count
        |> Iter.map_reduce(fn factory = factory, _n -> {
            Ok(#(robot, next)) = Factory.build(factory) else {
                unreachable "a new factory has names for many more robots"
            }
            #(Robot.name(robot), next)
        })

    names
}

group "robot name" {
    setup Factory.new(Seed.from_int(42))

    test "has a name", factory {
        assert Ok(#(robot, _factory)) = Factory.build(factory)
        assert well_formed?(Robot.name(robot))
    }

    test "name is the same each time", factory {
        assert Ok(#(robot, _factory)) = Factory.build(factory)
        assert Robot.name(robot) == Robot.name(robot)
    }

    test "different robots have different names", factory {
        assert Ok(#(first, factory)) = Factory.build(factory)
        assert Ok(#(second, _factory)) = Factory.build(factory)
        assert Robot.name(first) != Robot.name(second)
    }

    test "reset changes the name to a new well-formed one", factory {
        assert Ok(#(robot, factory)) = Factory.build(factory)
        assert Ok(#(reset, _factory)) = Factory.reset(factory, robot)
        assert Robot.name(reset) != Robot.name(robot)
        assert well_formed?(Robot.name(reset))
    }

    test "a thousand robots all have different names", factory {
        assert names(factory, 1000) |> Iter.to_set() |> Set.size() == 1000
    }

    test "the same seed names the same robots", factory {
        assert names(factory, 5) == names(Factory.new(Seed.from_int(42)), 5)
    }
}
```

## How it's written

- Adapted: the exercise asks for a robot object that names itself on first use and whose name a reset wipes in place, with uniqueness kept across every robot in the program. Nomi values do not change and there is no global state, so a `Factory` value holds what the exercise keeps hidden: the names given so far and the random seed. `Factory.build` answers a robot and the factory after it, and `Factory.reset` answers the robot named afresh and the factory after it. A robot is a value whose name never changes, so "the name is the same each time" holds by construction. The exercise has no canonical data, so the tests are the instructions' rules.
- Randomness is std/random's: a `Seed` threaded through `Generator.step`. The tests make the factory from a fixed seed, `Seed.from_int(42)`, so they are deterministic, and check properties (the format, different names, a thousand distinct names, the same seed giving the same names) rather than particular names.
- A name is one draw, `Generator.int` below 676,000 (26 × 26 × 1000), read as two letters and three digits, so every name is equally likely with no retry inside a name.
- A drawn name the factory has given before is drawn again. Once all 676,000 names are given, `build` answers `Error.NamesExhausted` rather than looping. A reset never gives back the robot's old name, nor any name given before, so `reset` needs only the factory; it takes the robot to say which one is reset.
- The tests are a `group` whose `setup` makes the factory, one test per rule. `names` builds many robots with `Iter.map_reduce` over the factory; a factory that runs out within a thousand robots would be a bug, which its `unreachable` says.
